name: Renal Cell Carcinoma, Stauffer Syndrome, and Partial Nephrectomy

reference.source: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22nd ed / Campbell-Walsh Urology 12th ed
clinicalPearls: Clear cell carcinoma represents 80% of RCC, arising from the proximal convoluted tubule with 3p VHL loss
Classic triad of flank pain, hematuria, and palpable mass occurs in under 10% due to incidental CT detection
Nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy is the gold standard for T1a tumors <= 4 cm, preserving renal reserve
A newly discovered left varicocele failing to decompress when recumbent suggests left renal vein tumor thrombus
Stauffer syndrome features reversible hepatic dysfunction in the absence of direct liver metastases
reference.pathophysiology: Renal cell carcinoma arises from tubular epithelium, most commonly proximal convoluted tubule cells characterized by lipid- and glycogen-rich clear cytoplasm. VHL tumor suppressor gene inactivation prevents ubiquitin-mediated degradation of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1alpha), driving constitutive overexpression of VEGF and PDGF that stimulates aggressive tumor angiogenesis and local vascular invasion.
additionalDifferentials: Renal oncocytoma (benign proximal tubular tumor with central spoke-wheel scar)
Renal angiomyolipoma (tuberous sclerosis association; microscopic fat on CT)
Transitional cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis
additionalInvestigations: Triple-phase contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis
Magnetic resonance venography / MRI if caval tumor thrombus is suspected
Chest computed tomography for staging pulmonary metastases
Serum calcium, alkaline phosphatase, liver function panel, and hemoglobin
